text: India has been successfully launching artificial satellites since 1975, with its space programme primarily managed by the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), which is responsible for designing, building, launching, and operating these satellites. Early Indian space missions began in the 1970s with Soviet assistance, launching the first two satellites. India achieved three consecutive successful satellite launches using its first-generation SLV rocket, and during this period, ISRO pursued two next-generation rocket projects based on SLV—ASLV and PSLV—but due to funding constraints and initial technical setbacks, ASLV was terminated after a few flights, and focus shifted entirely to PSLV. The PSLV, introduced in the 2000s, enabled India to become self-reliant in launching most of its remote sensing satellites. However, for heavy geostationary satellites, India remained dependent on European launchers until the 2000s, when indigenous capability to launch such satellites was developed. From the 2010s onward, India launched 27 geosynchronous/geostationary satellites—17 with indigenous launchers and 10 with European ones—achieving full self-reliance in this domain by the end of the decade. During this period, India also launched its first extra-terrestrial mission and became one of the few nations capable of launching Mars probes. ISRO improved student outreach by launching numerous pico-, nano-, and mini-satellites from Indian universities and established multiple bilateral collaborations with foreign research institutions. The decade also saw the completion of India’s regional navigation system, NAVIC. Increased subcontracting to private vendors boosted launch frequency by more than a factor of two, and ISRO successfully operationalized the Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) with an indigenous upper stage and the next-generation LVM3 with nearly double the payload capacity, enabling the launch of nearly all communication satellites. India launched Chandrayaan-2 in 2019, which failed to achieve a soft lunar landing, but demonstrated the capability to destroy enemy satellites in orbit. The decade witnessed a significant rise in the visibility of India’s space programme due to increased budget, improved payload capacity, reliability, launch frequency, and numerous firsts, including the 50th PSLV launch. In 2023, ISRO launched two extraterrestrial missions—Aditya L1 and Chandrayaan-3—while planning several others such as Chandrayaan-4, Lunar Polar Exploration Mission, Shukrayaan-1, and Mars Lander Mission, with proposed future missions to Jupiter and beyond the Solar System. The PSLV is expected to reach its 100th flight in the middle of the decade. India’s Small Satellite Launch Vehicle (SSLV) made its maiden flight on August 7, 2022, which failed, but SSLV-D2, launched on February 10, 2023, successfully deployed satellites, becoming the first SSLV to do so. The SCE-200 rocket engine, intended for India’s future heavy and super-heavy launch systems, is expected to make its first flight sometime in the middle of the decade. Orbital human spaceflight is the highest priority for ISRO, with long-term goals including crewed space stations and lunar landings. The list includes Indian satellites (wholly or partially owned, designed, or manufactured) operated by the government (ISRO, defence forces, other agencies) or private (educational and research) entities, excluding sub-orbital flights and foreign satellites launched by India. All successful launches are those that completed at least one full orbital flight. Data discrepancies are resolved by referencing N2YO and NASA NSSDCA, and orbital longitude applies only to geostationary and geosynchronous satellites. The table lists satellites in development and due for launch, and bar charts show decade-wise and vehicle-origin-based launch statistics. ISRO satellites launched by foreign agencies (Europe, USSR/Russia, United States) are separately listed. The following launch vehicle designations are included: L-03, V-24/L-23, V-51/423, V-58/429, V-81/453, V-97/468, V-117/486, V-128, V-147, V-160, V-162, V-169.
